idiom_name: Room @ForeignKey + explicit relations, or Jakarta @ManyToOne on the JVM
implementation_notes: Room refuses object references between entities: the entity stores the key (@ColumnInfo("author_id") val authorId: Long) and declares the constraint with @ForeignKey(entity = Author::class, parentColumns = ["id"], childColumns = ["author_id"]); the association is then read explicitly, either into an intermediate data class or as a multimap query result. On the JVM server side Kotlin uses the Jakarta annotations unchanged (@ManyToOne/@JoinColumn with data classes), so the provider resolves the key. Where Room is in use there is no mapper to replace - the join you write in the DAO, or the extra data class, is the deliberate stand-in for eager reference resolution.
pitfalls: Room forbids navigation across entities, so a relation that was not requested up front simply is not there: the compiler cannot notice that a screen started needing the author, only the DAO query can change.
foreignKeys only take effect when Room generates the schema; adding the annotation without a migration leaves existing tables unconstrained.
A non-suspend DAO function runs on the caller's thread - reading a relation from such a function on the main thread is exactly the disk-on-UI-thread query the design forbids.
